dailyBrief.text: Happy Halloween, Smileys — it's a cloudy, dry day in Solon, high near 59°, and it should be about 52–56° and dry for trick-or-treat from 6 to 8 tonight. Overnight, Iran said tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz while the U.S. insisted the main lanes are cleared, and Congo's Ebola outbreak passed 5,000 deaths. Today is a double-header: No. 2 Ohio State plays at USC at 7:30 PM with a freshman starting at quarterback, and the Cavs are in Milwaukee at 8. Locally, the North East Ohio Diwali Mela runs at 11 AM in Solon, early voting is open 8 AM to 4 PM in Cleveland, and don't forget the clocks fall back tonight — an extra hour of sleep before the Browns play for first place tomorrow.

Election week dominates the calendar — early voting ends Sunday 1–5 PM, then polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM for the governor's race, the Husted–Brown Senate fight and every statewide office; note that 66 Cuyahoga precincts have moved, so check your location before Tuesday. The standout deal is still Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through November 4 — and with the baby due in early November, this is officially any-day-now week at home.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
U.S. and Iran race to revive Qatar talks — and Trump may weigh new strikes after the midterms
items.summary:
Qatari mediators spent more than 12 hours in Tehran on Friday trying to keep a U.S.-Iran deal alive before Tuesday's midterm elections, and a U.S. delegation is now expected to join indirect talks in Qatar. A diplomatic source described the Tehran session as showing positive progress, though no agreement has been announced.

Reporting based on Axios says the two sides have discussed preliminary steps on Iran's nuclear program and on the Strait of Hormuz, where a U.S. fleet has been escorting tankers. One draft idea would have Iran transfer its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to an agreed third country, with financial incentives for Tehran also discussed.

The risk is what happens if diplomacy stalls. A U.S. official told Axios the president could be more inclined to order a major military operation if Republicans lose badly on Tuesday, while a White House official pushed back and said the election results would not drive decisions on Iran. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned Washington on Saturday not to strike again, and the last U.S. strike came in September.

Watch whether the Doha talks produce a written framework this weekend, and whether either side pauses military moves until after the vote.

items.title: Spain's train-crash inquiry points to four system failures as mourning enters a third day
items.summary:
Spain marked a third day of national mourning on Saturday for the 69 people killed when two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in Toledo province, on Wednesday. Families gathered near the crash area while officials worked through a difficult identification process, with dozens of missing-person reports still active and 39 people still in hospital in Castilla-La Mancha.

An infrastructure report cited in new coverage points to as many as four system failures before the crash. The central one was a failure of the LZB safety system at Urda, which is meant to keep two trains from occupying the same stretch of track, after a Renfe train was told the line ahead was clear and ran into a stopped Iryo train.

Among the dead were a former employment minister, Fatima Banez, and a 24-year-old athlete, Julieta Gallego. The drivers' union has asked for a full review of the rules that apply when automatic protection systems fail.

This was Spain's second major rail disaster this year, which is why a technical failure is quickly becoming a political one. Watch for the formal investigation findings and whether the government orders network-wide safety changes.

items.title: Israel's election ends in deadlock — here are the four ways out
items.summary:
Final results in Israel confirm no winner. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot won 48, and Arab-led parties won a record 19 between them — leaving every path to the 61 seats needed to govern running through difficult partners.

The options are narrow. The opposition could try to govern with Arab-party support, which several of its own leaders oppose. It could seek a national unity government with Netanyahu, which Eisenkot has ruled out. Party leaders could replace key Knesset posts and constrain a caretaker government, or the talks could fail entirely and send Israelis back to the polls.

Turnout was 77.9 percent, the highest in decades, with more than 5.7 million ballots cast. Likud remained the largest single party with 27 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar with 21.

President Isaac Herzog is due to receive the formal results on November 4 and then assign one leader 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to form a government. Watch who gets the first attempt.

items.title: Nigeria investigates two suspected Ebola cases in its northeast as Congo's toll passes 5,000
items.summary:
Nigeria's disease-control agency said on Saturday that it is investigating two suspected Ebola cases in the country's northeast. Both people have been isolated while officials trace contacts and run laboratory tests, and the agency stressed that neither case is confirmed yet.

The alert lands as the wider regional outbreak deepens. Congo's government data this week put Ebola deaths there above 5,000, and cases have already been reported in Kenya, Uganda and now possibly Nigeria — a sign the outbreak is moving along travel and trade routes rather than staying in one place.

Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, so even a suspected case triggers a fast, visible response: isolation, contact listing and testing before any confirmation. That is the system working as designed, but it also shows how much surveillance the region now needs at once.

Watch for the laboratory results. A confirmed case in Nigeria would widen the outbreak's footprint significantly; two negative tests would still leave the regional picture unchanged.

items.title: China's factories shrink again in October, at the fastest pace in three months
items.summary:
China's official manufacturing survey fell to 49.3 in October, down from 50.1 in September and below the 50 line that separates growth from contraction. It was the fastest pace of shrinkage in three months, according to the National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters.

The survey tracks whether purchasing managers see conditions improving or worsening across new orders, output and employment. October's reading pointed to soft demand both at home and for exports — the two engines Chinese factories rely on when one of them sputters.

A contracting factory sector in the world's largest manufacturer matters well beyond China. It signals weaker orders for suppliers across Asia and softer demand for commodities and shipping worldwide.

Watch the private-sector version of the survey and any fresh stimulus signals from Beijing, which together will show whether October was a dip or the start of a longer slide.

items.title: A tanker is hit by limpet mines in Hormuz — the first attack of its kind since 2019
items.summary:
A small boat approached a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday night and attached two explosive devices to its hull, about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab in Oman. The blasts set off an engine-room fire that was later put out, the crew stayed safe, and the ship continued toward anchorage off the United Arab Emirates coast.

The incident sits alongside wider Iranian claims. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said several tankers had hit mines or been halted after trying a southern route Tehran calls unauthorized, and Oman's navy evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged merchant ship that caught fire off Musandam. U.S. Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper said the main internationally recognized transit routes have been cleared of mines and that dozens of commercial vessels are moving through.

October has been the heaviest month for attacks on shipping since the war began in February, and the return of limpet mines — last used in the Gulf in 2019 — marks a change in tactics. The strait once carried about a fifth of the world's energy, so each new method of stopping ships raises the risk for crews and for oil prices.

Watch for confirmation of which vessels were involved and whether more tankers pause or reroute while the Qatar talks continue.

items.title: A judge bars the Justice Department from threatening election workers over ballots it calls ineligible
items.summary:
A federal judge in San Francisco ruled late Friday that the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security may not threaten election workers with criminal prosecution over how they handle ballots. Judge Trina Thompson's temporary order also bars the departments from demanding that officials set aside, refuse or stop processing a registered voter's ballot solely because the government alleges that voter is ineligible.

The case was brought by labor unions and civil-rights groups, including SEIU, AFSCME, LULAC and the NAACP. The Justice Department had demanded that California set aside about 20,000 ballots and Washington 405, and prosecutors had subpoenaed Los Angeles County election workers to a grand jury.

The order runs until November 16 and requires the departments to notify every government that received their ballot letters that the threats are blocked. A preliminary-injunction hearing is set for November 13, and the department must respond by noon Monday.

With voting already underway and Election Day on Tuesday, the ruling means local officials keep following state procedures for counting ballots unless a court says otherwise.

items.title: Four days before the election, the Justice Department opens a case on Arizona voter-registration groups
items.summary:
The U.S. Attorney for Arizona, Timothy Courchaine, announced Friday that his office has opened a case into reporting about three non-profit organizations accused of registering non-citizens to vote, and has already referred the matter to the FBI. The groups are Stand Indivisible Arizona, Worker Power and When We Count, a registration program tied to the Democratic National Committee.

On October 26, Courchaine wrote to Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes asking them to review registrations connected to the three groups. Axios reported the underlying material was an undercover video in which people posing as a non-citizen and as a felon on probation asked canvassers about registering; the exercises were stopped before any form was submitted, and a DNC spokesperson called the allegations fabricated.

No charges have been announced, and the announcement does not establish that any illegal registration occurred. Arizona's registration deadline had already passed weeks earlier.

The timing — four days before a midterm in a closely watched state — is the story as much as the allegations. Watch for responses from the three groups and from state election officials this weekend.

items.title: Talk of martial law on a pro-Trump activist call draws a hard legal reality check
items.summary:
Advocates on a partisan activist call in late September floated an extraordinary idea: using martial law and federal seizure of ballots or voting equipment if the midterms were deemed rigged. The suggestion, attributed in Axios reporting to longtime Trump associate Peter Ticktin, has resurfaced in coverage this weekend as lawsuits and disputes pile up around the election.

Legal experts quoted in the coverage make a consistent point: U.S. elections are run by the states under federal guardrails, and neither emergency powers nor the Insurrection Act gives a president authority to commandeer ballots or machines. The Defense Department has also disavowed any role deploying troops to polling places or seizing election materials.

There is no evidence in the reporting that vote-counting systems are deleting or changing votes. The lawful tools after a disputed election are audits, recounts, canvasses and litigation — slow, public processes rather than seizures.

Why it matters is trust: talk of seizing ballots, even as a hypothetical, shapes how supporters on both sides may receive Tuesday's results. Watch for whether any official adopts the idea, which would move it from rhetoric to a court fight.

items.title: Hegseth fires a top Pentagon planner after an investigation into leaks on Iran and Ukraine
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff's director of strategy, plans and policy, on Thursday after an Air Force investigation found he had leaked classified information about U.S. policy on Iran and Ukraine to reporters. Reporting based on Axios says Sylvia admitted to the leaks on video after failing polygraph tests, and the case has been referred to the Justice Department.

Investigators say the leaking began as early as June 2025. According to the report, Sylvia took notes while reviewing a classified report on U.S. assistance to Ukraine and passed information to a reporter over the Signal app and at a diner in Arlington, Virginia, about ten minutes from the Pentagon. That reporter was writing a book.

The same reporting says Sylvia acknowledged being one of about 20 officials who had criticized Hegseth's leadership in the press. Accounts differ on whether he failed three or four polygraphs.

A three-star officer in charge of strategy leaking war policy is a serious breach case on its own terms, and a Justice Department referral means it may not end with his firing. Watch for whether charges or a court-martial follow.

items.title: The midterms arrive under a pileup of lawsuits and ballot disputes
items.summary:
The 2026 midterms already face a messy pileup of lawsuits and ballot battles, raising fears about election confidence before voters even finish casting ballots, Axios reports. Fights are running in parallel over voter lists, mail-ballot rules and how certification will work after Tuesday.

Election challenges on their own are not unusual. What is different this cycle, in the reporting, is the volume combined with continued false claims about widespread voter fraud from the administration, which leaves state and local officials juggling court orders and federal demands at the same time as they run the vote.

This weekend alone has produced a restraining order against the Justice Department over threats to election workers and a new federal case on voter-registration groups in Arizona. Each ruling changes, at least temporarily, what officials may or may not do with ballots in the final days.

Watch the Monday deadlines: several courts have responses due the day before Election Day, and any late ruling could still change procedures in specific states.

items.title: Democrats take an 8-to-9-point generic-ballot lead into the final weekend
items.summary:
Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by roughly 8 to 9 points heading into the final weekend before Tuesday's midterms, according to the polling roundup in Saturday coverage, and they are spending heavily even in districts the president carried by 20 points in 2024.

A generic-ballot lead that large would normally point to a strong night for the out party, but the voters who have not yet cast ballots are polling much closer to tied. That split is why both parties are treating turnout — not persuasion — as the whole game over the next three days.

The same Saturday roundup noted House members asking the administration to preserve presidential chats with the Grok AI system, and the Pentagon quietly updating the Iran war death toll to 23. Campaigns on both sides spent Saturday at rallies and in early-vote lines rather than rolling out new policy.

Ohio is a live test of the national picture: early voting ends Sunday, and both the governor's race and a Senate race there have polled close. Watch final turnout reports Sunday night for the last hard numbers before Tuesday.

items.title: The Nasdaq 100 slides into its third correction of the year as AI spending spooks investors
items.summary:
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite finished Friday down 2.86 percent, its worst single day since June, and the Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 4.5 percent intraday — enough to put it in its third correction of the year. October wiped out roughly $2 trillion of value from the index.

The trigger was a week of earnings that told one story from several companies: a great deal of money is going into artificial intelligence and not enough is visibly coming back yet. Alphabet had its worst day ever on Thursday, losing about $475 billion in value after search growth slowed and free cash flow swung to a loss of about $9 billion. Amazon fell after reporting even heavier AI spending and slower growth in its shopping business.

Chip and cloud names sold off together. CoreWeave lost 37 percent in October and Nebius nearly 35 percent, as investors questioned the debt loads behind the data-center buildout.

No single stock caused this; it is a repricing of the AI trade itself. Watch whether Monday's session, on the eve of the midterms, steadies or extends the slide.

items.title: Intel's worst day since 1974 leads the rout — and money rotates into defensive stocks
items.summary:
Intel sank almost 29 percent on Friday, erasing roughly $140 billion in market value in one session, after its fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $15 to $16 billion came in well below the $17.1 billion analysts expected. It was the chipmaker's worst day since 1974, and it happened even though its third-quarter results beat expectations.

The rest of the market followed tech down but not as far. The S&P 500 fell 1.82 percent to 7,580.07 and the Dow lost 1.09 percent to 51,770.31, with defensive sectors limiting the damage. AMD fell about 11 percent, Nvidia around 4 percent and Broadcom about 5 percent, while SanDisk slid 13 percent despite beating estimates.

Sentiment took another hit from a report that Blackstone has told investors Anthropic may not secure an investment-grade rating at its market debut, cooling some of the optimism that followed the AI company's S-1 filing earlier in the week.

Rotation into defensives ahead of an election usually signals caution rather than panic. Watch credit markets and Anthropic's debut pricing for whether that caution deepens.

items.title: Binance says it has replaced 90 percent of the $6.3 billion hack — withdrawals due Sunday
items.summary:
Binance said on Saturday that it has replaced about 90 percent of the roughly $6.3 billion in crypto stolen from its hot wallets on Thursday, using company money and emergency reserves. Balances in ten major tokens — including bitcoin, ether, USDT, BNB and SOL — are now fully backed, the exchange said.

Withdrawals, paused since the hack, remain on track to reopen in phases on Sunday, November 1, subject to security checks. Binance published a new proof-of-reserves snapshot taken at midnight UTC on October 31 showing coverage of 100 percent or more for the named tokens, with the full cryptographic proof that lets users verify their own balances expected by November 3.

Replacing the money is not the same as recovering it. About $3 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen with help from law enforcement and partners, and analytics firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Binance first pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop and later said investigators had found additional breach points.

Sunday is the test: a smooth phased reopening would calm customers; any delay would renew questions about the largest crypto theft on record.

items.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17 billion — and one membership would cover both
items.summary:
DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart's parent, Maplebear, for about $17 billion, or $65 a share — a 26 percent premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, before reports of a possible deal. At least 75 percent of the price will be paid in cash, funded from DoorDash's reserves and new debt.

DoorDash says Instacart will keep its brand, app and the technology products it sells to grocers. For customers, the headline promise is a single membership covering both DashPass and Instacart+, which the company estimates would save members about $100 million a year, and access to tens of thousands more stores across the two platforms.

The deal was announced alongside record DoorDash results: third-quarter revenue up 34 percent to $4.62 billion, with total orders up 28 percent to 993 million. Instacart cancelled its scheduled November 5 earnings call after the agreement.

Nothing changes yet for shoppers. The acquisition needs antitrust clearance in the U.S. plus approvals in Canada and Israel, and is not expected to close until late 2027 or the first half of 2028.

items.title: The Fed tilts toward a December rate hike — and what comes next hinges on oil
items.summary:
The Federal Reserve's October 28 statement shifted the central bank toward another rate increase in December, according to market pricing tracked after the meeting. CME FedWatch readings cited in analysis this week put a December hike firmly in play after officials held rates steady in October.

The hinge variable is oil. Prices swung more than $2 in a day this week on news of a Qatari draft proposal for Iran and a senior Iranian official's dismissal of it, and every move in energy feeds directly into the inflation data the Fed is watching. Brent has pushed toward $117 a barrel during the Hormuz shipping crisis.

For households, a December hike would keep mortgage and credit-card rates elevated into the new year, even as the job market and the election dominate headlines. For markets, it adds a policy headwind on top of the AI-stock selloff.

Watch oil first and the Fed second: a Hormuz settlement that drops crude would change the December math faster than any speech.

items.title: AI spending tops $700 billion this year — investors are asking what it buys
items.summary:
Four major technology companies have committed more than $700 billion to artificial-intelligence infrastructure this year, a sum comparable to the GDP of Argentina or Belgium. This week's selloff was the market's answer so far: spending at that scale, without returns to match, gets repriced.

The details behind the doubt are concrete. Amazon spent more than $77 billion on data centers, servers and warehouses in a single quarter, pushing its trailing free cash flow to negative $42.4 billion. Alphabet's quarterly equipment purchases topped $51 billion. Analysts note that chip capacity sold each quarter roughly doubled every nine months from early 2024 to mid-2026 — supply growing that fast eventually meets demand.

None of this means the buildout stops. The companies racing to build AI capacity still describe it as existential, and cloud revenue is genuinely growing — Amazon's AWS rose 39 percent in the quarter.

The question for the next earnings season is narrower: can any of the big spenders show AI revenue catching up with AI cost? Watch capital-spending guidance, not headlines, for the answer.

items.title: One killed and six hurt in a shooting inside a California Spirit Halloween store
items.summary:
A gunman opened fire inside a packed Spirit Halloween store at the Solano Town Center mall in Fairfield, California, on Friday evening, killing one person and wounding six others as shoppers bought last-minute costumes. Three of the wounded are in critical condition, according to authorities.

A survivor described running from the shots, which rang out around 8:30 p.m. in the seasonal pop-up store. SWAT teams swept the mall, including a cinema where about a dozen people were watching a horror film, and the FBI's Sacramento office sent its evidence response team to help local police.

Fairfield police said Saturday afternoon that a single individual carried out what they consider a targeted incident. The scene remains active, detectives are interviewing witnesses, and police have not released a description of the suspect or the identities of the victims. A manhunt is underway.

A targeted shooting in a crowded holiday store raises the questions investigators are working now: who was the intended victim, and is the suspect still nearby? Watch for a suspect description and any arrest announcement from Fairfield police.

items.title: Truckers are asked to check dashcams as the manhunt for an escaped Tennessee murderer widens
items.summary:
The search for Jacob Allen Morley, 28, entered its sixth day on Saturday. Morley, serving a life sentence for the 2022 killing of his coworker Cody Birchfield, escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, late on October 25, and a truck he is accused of stealing was found abandoned in Marion, Illinois, two days later.

The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation has now asked truck drivers who were at the Pilot Travel Center on Vernell Road in Marion on Monday, October 26, between 5 and 7 a.m. to review their dashcam footage for any sign of him. Investigators are also examining a possible connection to a Wisconsin bank robbery, though Morley has not been confirmed as a suspect in it.

The combined reward for information leading to his capture stands at $17,500. Morley is described as about 6 feet tall and 240 to 270 pounds, with green eyes and brown hair, and officials say he is considered dangerous and could be anywhere.

Anyone who sees him is told not to approach and to call 911, or the TBI at 1-800-TBI-FIND. Watch for dashcam identifications, which are now the investigation's most specific public lead.

items.title: Clocks fall back at 2 a.m. Sunday — and the bill to end the switch is stuck in the Senate
items.summary:
Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, November 1, when most of the country sets clocks back one hour and gains an extra hour of sleep. Only Hawaii and most of Arizona skip the change. Sunset on Sunday will come an hour earlier — in many places before 5 p.m.

The twice-yearly switch may be living on borrowed time, but not this year. The Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent, passed the House in July and has stalled in the Senate during the election recess. The president supports it and publicly accused Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas of holding it up; Cotton replied that Congress tried permanent daylight time before and reversed course.

The bill faces a hard deadline: pending legislation expires in early January, when the lawmakers elected on Tuesday take office. If it dies, a new Congress would have to start over.

Practically, tonight is the night to change the clocks that do not change themselves — ovens, cars and wall clocks — before bed. Daylight time returns on March 14, 2027, under current law.

items.title: Notre Dame and Villanova open the college basketball season in Rome — with the pope's blessing
items.summary:
College basketball starts its season in an unusual place on Sunday: the Palazzo dello Sport in Rome, where Notre Dame and Villanova meet in the Eternal City Tip-Off, a men's and women's doubleheader. The men's game tips at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, followed by the women at noon, with Notre Dame's women entering ranked No. 13.

Pope Leo XIV met both universities' teams at the Vatican on Saturday. The event connects to the pope's own Villanova background, and thousands of supporters have traveled to Rome for a season opener that looks nothing like a typical opening weekend on a campus.

International openers are rare in college basketball, and this one doubles as a showcase for the sport abroad at the very start of the season. Both schools get a marquee stage; both also accept the travel and time-zone costs that come with it.

Watch the women's game for an early read on a ranked Notre Dame team, and the crowd — a sellout in Rome would make this experiment an annual conversation.

items.title: Halloween night: dry and mild for most of the East, wet for parts of the West and Plains
items.summary:
Trick-or-treaters across the Northeast, Great Lakes and much of the East get the good draw tonight: dry weather, light winds and evening temperatures in the 50s and 60s, several degrees above normal for the last night of October.

The trouble spots are west and south. Showers and thunderstorms could soak parts of Texas and the Plains, with heavy rain possible from South Texas toward Kansas and a flash-flood risk where downpours repeat. Southern California and the Southwest could see rain by evening, with snow possible in the Rockies and the Sierra Nevada, and scattered showers from Arkansas and Louisiana to the Carolinas and South Florida.

The chilliest air sits across Montana, Idaho, Wyoming and the inland Northwest, where wind chills in the 30s and 40s will make costumes feel thin. Solon sits in the comfortable group: cloudy but dry, with temperatures in the low-to-mid 50s during trick-or-treat hours.

One timing note for tonight's plans everywhere: this is the last evening of daylight saving time, so tomorrow's sunset arrives before 5 p.m. in New York, Chicago, Denver, Los Angeles and Seattle alike.

items.title: A Halloween that falls on the clock change won't happen again until 2037
items.summary:
This weekend's overlap of Halloween and the end of daylight saving time is rarer than it feels. The last time the two coincided was 2020, and because of how leap years shift the calendar in 2028, 2032 and 2036, Halloween will not fall on a Saturday — or on the clock-change weekend — again until 2037.

For this year, the overlap is a bonus rather than a disruption: the clock change happens at 2 a.m. Sunday, after trick-or-treating is over, so Halloween night itself runs on the usual schedule and everyone simply gets an extra hour afterward — to stay out later or to sleep it off.

Maryland coverage of the weekend notes the same mechanics that apply nationally: phones and computers update themselves, while analog clocks, appliances and car dashboards need a manual turn-back before bed on Halloween night.

If your household has a young child, the less festive side arrives Sunday: sleep schedules tend to wobble for a few days after the fall-back, even with the extra hour. Earlier light in the morning and darker evenings are the trade until March.

items.title: OHSAA says it will comply with the court order putting Glenville back in the playoffs
items.summary:
The Ohio High School Athletic Association issued a formal statement late Friday on the Glenville football dispute. The association said it stands by its Thursday ruling removing Cleveland Glenville from the playoffs, but that it will comply with the court order requiring the Glenville-University School playoff game to be played, and is working with both schools to reschedule it this weekend.

A Cuyahoga County judge granted Glenville student-athletes a temporary restraining order on Friday. The case began when the OHSAA requested student residential information from the Cleveland Metropolitan School District on September 28 and received an initial batch on October 22; at a Thursday meeting, the association says, Glenville did not object to the audit's findings.

University School has been reported as not planning to take part in the matchup, which is why rescheduling — rather than simply playing at the original time — is now the work in front of both schools. Glenville, 8-2 and the defending state champion in its division, is chasing a fourth state title in five years.

A hearing is scheduled for Monday, one day before Election Day and in the middle of the playoff calendar. Watch whether the game actually gets played this weekend, and what Monday's hearing does to the bracket.

items.title: Browns get a double boost for Pittsburgh: Tytus Howard cleared and Mike Hall Jr. back
items.summary:
Cleveland's injury picture brightened on Saturday. Starting right tackle Tytus Howard cleared concussion protocol and carries no injury designation into Sunday's game at Pittsburgh, after missing practice all week. The Browns also elevated rookie tight end Carsen Ryan from the practice squad for the game.

On defense, tackle Mike Hall Jr. returns after missing three weeks with the ankle injury he suffered in the first Steelers meeting — a game in which he came back to record his only sack of the season. Head coach Todd Monken's group has leaned on its defensive front all year, allowing 20.9 points per game.

The stakes are plain: both teams are 5-2, Cleveland won the first meeting 27-24 on October 1, and a win Sunday gives the Browns the season sweep and sole possession of first place in the AFC North. Quarterback Deshaun Watson is coming off a 308-yard game in the 27-24 comeback at Tennessee.

The remaining question mark is slot corner Myles Harden, listed as questionable with a hamstring injury. Watch the final inactive list Sunday morning.

items.title: Cavs at Milwaukee tonight: Harden and Mitchell lead Cleveland into its first division test
items.summary:
The Cleveland Cavaliers (3-2) play the Milwaukee Bucks (1-4) tonight at 8 p.m. Eastern at Fiserv Forum, their first Central Division matchup of the season, coming off a close loss in Atlanta on Thursday. Cleveland's expected starters are James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen.

Milwaukee is a rebuilding team after trading Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami this summer, and it has given up 127 or more points in four of its five games. Tyler Herro, acquired in that trade, now leads the Bucks at 23.4 points per game, with Myles Turner still anchoring the middle.

Mitchell leads Cleveland at 24.2 points, 5.6 rebounds and 4.8 assists per game, while Mobley adds 18.2 points and 8.8 rebounds. Oddsmakers have the Cavs favored by roughly nine points. On the injury list, Meleek Thomas and Jaylon Tyson are questionable and Nae'Qwan Tomlin is out; Milwaukee's report is clean.

Cleveland has been unbeaten at home and winless on the road so far — tonight is the chance to fix the second half of that sentence. The Cavs then host Oklahoma City on Monday.

items.title: Ohio State at USC tonight: a freshman quarterback, the nation's stingiest defense, and first place on the line
items.summary:
No. 2 Ohio State (6-1, 4-0 Big Ten) plays at USC (6-2) tonight at 7:30 p.m. Eastern on NBC, in the programs' first meeting as conference opponents and Ohio State's first visit to the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum since 2008. True freshman Luke Fahey is expected to make his first collegiate start, with starting quarterback Julian Sayin out after injuring his throwing arm at Indiana on October 17.

The Buckeyes' defense is the reason they travel as roughly a touchdown favorite anyway: it allows just 13.4 points and 264.3 yards per game, and held defending champion Indiana to 15 points in Ohio State's last outing. Fahey's top target is Jeremiah Smith, who has 52 catches for 984 yards and 12 touchdowns.

USC counters with quarterback Jayden Maiava, who has thrown for 2,303 yards and 19 touchdowns, but the Trojans are coming off a 24-7 loss at Wisconsin in which they managed minus-17 rushing yards. Staff predictions collected this morning cluster around a one-to-two-score Ohio State win.

A win keeps Ohio State unbeaten in the Big Ten and in control of its title path. Watch Fahey's first two drives — the game plan will show quickly how much the coaches trust him.

items.title: Ohio's governor's race stays a coin flip: polls split, prediction markets favor Acton
items.summary:
The race between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for Ohio governor remains genuinely undecided three days before the election. A Marist poll in mid-October put Acton ahead 50 to 43; a later Echelon Insights poll put Ramaswamy ahead 47 to 45 — both inside or near their margins of error.

Prediction markets are less equivocal: Acton trades around 68 percent on Kalshi and 72 percent on Polymarket in the latest readings, meaning traders see her as the clear, if not certain, favorite. The state Republican chairman, meanwhile, told Newsmax this week that the party's early-vote tracking shows no Democratic wave in Ohio.

The Senate race on the same ballot is nearly as close, with Marist showing former senator Sherrod Brown ahead of incumbent Jon Husted 48 to 44. Both statewide races are why Ohio is drawing national attention and money in the final weekend.

With no further debate scheduled, the closing contest is turnout. Watch which campaign's voters show up in the final early-voting session on Sunday.

items.title: Final weekend of Ohio early voting: today until 4, Sunday 1 to 5 — then Tuesday decides it
items.summary:
Early in-person voting in Ohio is in its final weekend. Polls at county boards of elections were open until 4 p.m. today, and the last session runs Sunday from 1 to 5 p.m. After that, the only way to vote is in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.

Turnout has run well ahead of the last midterm in much of the state. Licking County, one example tracked this month, was averaging more than 700 early voters a day and on pace to shatter its 2018 and 2022 early totals, and more than 920,000 Ohioans had voted early as of October 23.

Cuyahoga County voters should double-check their Election Day location before Tuesday: 66 precincts in the county have moved. The statewide ballot also includes Issue 3, a proposed constitutional amendment requiring photo identification at the polls. In Cleveland today, voting got a Halloween twist, with a Pull Up to the Polls block party outside the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections.

Anyone still holding an absentee ballot should check the county board's return guidance today rather than Monday — after Sunday, deadlines, not intentions, decide whether it counts.

baby.tip: Do the final hospital-bag sweep together this weekend: IDs and insurance cards in the front pocket, phone chargers and a long cable, snacks for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in newborn and 0–3 month sizes — babies pick their own size. Then leave the bag by the door, not in a closet, so nobody is packing at 3 AM.
baby.fact: Newborns see best at about 8 to 12 inches from their face — almost exactly the distance to a parent's face during a feed — and they already recognize their mother's voice from hearing it in the womb. High-contrast black-and-white patterns are the first 'pictures' a new baby can really study.
